questions.prompt: Is there a defect in how this code handles refresh token reuse? If so, mark the line(s) where it is; otherwise answer that there is none.
Refresh tokens are 32 random bytes and only their SHA-256 hash is stored. What does that protect against?
choices: Replay of a stolen token, because the hash changes on every request.
Forgery of access tokens, because the hash is used as the JWT signing key.
Someone who reads the refresh_tokens table getting values they can present to the refresh endpoint.
Expiry bypass, because the hash includes the expiry time.

questions.prompt: findByTokenHash is declared with @Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE). Two refresh requests with the same, still unused token arrive at the same time. What does the lock accomplish?
choices: The second request waits until the first commits, then sees the token as used instead of also rotating it.
Both requests rotate successfully, and each gets a different new token in the same family.
It stops two different employees from logging in at once.
It guarantees the access token returned to both callers is identical.

questions.prompt: An employee is deactivated in the HR directory. They hold an unused, unexpired refresh token and an access token issued five minutes ago. What happens?
choices: The refresh succeeds once more because the directory is only consulted at login.
The refresh is rejected and the whole token family is revoked.
The refresh is rejected and the access token is invalidated immediately.
The refresh is rejected with InvalidTokenException, but the access token stays valid until its 15-minute expiry because nothing checks the directory on each request.
